analysis.one_liner: Lets the FDA regulate cigarettes and tobacco products, with tougher warnings and ad limits.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 127 cosponsors from both parties, including the House's top Democrat, but never left the House Energy and Commerce subcommittee and never got a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Supreme Court ruled in 2000 that the FDA lacked authority over tobacco, this bill would have written that authority into law: nicotine in a tobacco product would count as a drug, and tobacco products as devices, under federal food and drug law. Within 18 months the government would have to issue strong rotating health warnings matching the 1997 tobacco settlement's proposed specs, companies could not claim a product was 'reduced risk' without FDA proof, and ad and sales restrictions would apply to every retailer, including tobacco-only shops. It also would have revived the FDA's voided 1996 rules on youth access and advertising.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone exposed to tobacco marketing and secondhand smoke, and especially minors, who would face renewed FDA rules on youth access and advertising; smokers, who would get stronger, rotating warnings and honest risk claims; and state health officials, who would gain a federal partner in policing cigarette marketing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Smokers, minors, and people breathing secondhand smoke

how_it_helps.text: Defines nicotine in a tobacco product as a drug and tobacco products as devices, giving the FDA direct regulatory authority the Supreme Court said it did not have.

Requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to issue regulations, within 18 months, mandating strong rotating warnings on cigarette and smokeless tobacco labels and ads, conforming to the 1997 settlement's proposed specifications.
Bars manufacturers from claiming or implying a product is 'reduced risk' unless the FDA has determined it actually presents a significantly reduced risk to public health.
Lets the FDA restrict tobacco advertising and promotion, and requires those restrictions to apply uniformly to all retailers, including stores that sell almost nothing but tobacco.
Gives the FDA enforcement power over tobacco violations and the authority to compel testimony and documents, with disclosure to the public when needed to protect health.
Makes the FDA's voided 1996 tobacco regulations take legal effect one year after enactment, restoring its rules on youth access and advertising.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers, who would face FDA oversight, restricted marketing, new warning requirements, and enforcement actions. Smokers could eventually see some of those compliance costs passed through in prices. Tobacco growers and warehouses would pay nothing, since the bill explicitly exempts them.

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts states from requiring any health warning on cigarette packages or ads beyond the federal ones, locking states into whatever the federal standard turns out to be.

It exempts tobacco leaf, growers, warehouses, and grower cooperatives from FDA authority entirely, and bars FDA inspectors from a grower's farm without written consent, so raw tobacco production stays unregulated.
It validates the FDA's 1996 rules as written rather than requiring fresh rulemaking, baking in a decade-old regulatory approach, and it regulates tobacco rather than reducing or eliminating its use.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health gains are large: a 400,000-deaths-a-year product would finally face the same basic oversight as any other consumable, with honest warnings and restricted youth marketing. The compromises are real but narrower than the gains: state warning preemption is a genuine loss for stronger state rules, and the grower carve-out leaves leaf production untouched. On balance a well-designed, if imperfect, public health measure.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee on April 2, 2001, and sat there with no hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 20, 2001 by Rep. Greg Ganske with 49 original cosponsors from both parties, including Rep. John Dingell, the ranking Democrat on Energy and Commerce.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
On April 2, 2001 it was referred to the Health Subcommittee, and the record shows no further action on the bill for the rest of the 107th Congress.
The bill accumulated 127 cosponsors: 103 of 208 House Democrats, 23 of 223 House Republicans, and the chamber's one Independent.
The Congress adjourned January 3, 2003 with the bill still in subcommittee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers, who kept operating free of FDA oversight for the rest of the decade; Congress did not grant the FDA tobacco authority until the 2009 tobacco control law.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship crossed party lines: the bill was sponsored by a Republican, cosponsored by the chamber's most senior House Democrat, and backed by 103 of 208 House Democrats, 23 of 223 House Republicans, and the chamber's lone Independent.

industries.note: The bill would subject them to FDA oversight, mandatory rotating warnings, honest reduced-risk claims, and enforceable ad and marketing restrictions for the first time. Its interest in killing the bill ran against the public's interest in regulating the leading cause of preventable death.

industries.industry: Tobacco growers, warehouses, and grower cooperatives
industries.note: The bill explicitly exempts leaf tobacco and its producers from FDA authority and bars FDA inspectors from farms without written consent, locking in an unregulated upstream segment even as manufacturers come under oversight. That shields a rural industry from costs without directly opposing the public health rules downstream.
Ad and sales restrictions would apply to every retailer, with no special exemption for stores that sell only tobacco, closing a common loophole in youth-access laws.

industries.industry: State governments as public health regulators
industries.note: Once federal warnings exist, states could not require stricter health statements on packages or ads, consolidating the warning standard at the federal level even if states wanted to go further.
